clue.text: Achieves easy success, when not yielding to highwayman's request?

definitions.meaning: to triumph without effort, as a racehorse once did when its jockey could drop his ...

definitions.text: when not yielding to highwayman's request?
definitions.meaning: someone refusing keeps their arms lowered

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is whimsical: a robber's classic order is 'Hands up!', so defiance is the opposite position.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to win comfortably, from jockeys relaxing their grip on the reins when well ahead.

clue.text: Good old England wicketkeeper who worked for TV programme?

parts.note: Les Ames kept wicket for England in the 1920s and 30s

indicators.note: worked suggests the letters of the little word who have been kneaded into a new order

explanation.surface: A question about which former England cricketer went on to make a television show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worked' shuffles WHO into HOW. Les Ames was a Kent and England wicketkeeper-batsman; cricket's wicketkeeper stands behind the stumps.
explanation.definitionFit: A quiz or contest broadcast for entertainment is a classic example of a television programme genre.

clue.text: Sort of business catastrophe to get caught up in

annotationWithheld.why: Sort of business catastrophe to get caught up in (3-3): DOOM (catastrophe) needs TC inside to give DOTCOM, and no reading of 'to get caught up' supplies T and C in that order; no blog found to confirm the setter's parse
annotationWithheld.clue: Sort of business catastrophe to get caught up in

clue.text: Stars joining jail birds

parts.note: can is slang for prison
Aries is a constellation, a group of stars

explanation.surface: Celebrities find themselves locked up alongside other inmates.
explanation.walkthrough: The charade is in answer order: the jail piece comes first though 'Stars' leads the clue; 'joining' simply links them.
explanation.definitionFit: Canaries are small yellow finches kept as songbirds, so they are a kind of bird.

clue.text: Top gymnast in Eastern city once

parts.note: PE, physical education, is the school subject of gymnasts, giving the letters for the gym
the king is the top person in a realm

explanation.surface: A champion gymnast competes in a city in the Far East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top gymnast' reads as the king of PE, the school gym lesson, with the pieces in answer order.
explanation.definitionFit: Peking is the old Western name for Beijing, the Chinese capital, hence a city of the East formerly so called.

clue.text: Got lucre quickly with fancy backed — a fat sum

indicators.note: fancy as an adjective means elaborate or fanciful, telling us the following letters are dressed up in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone backed a favourite horse and pocketed a large sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' rearranges BACKED A FAT SUM, thirteen letters, into the phrase. 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes earning money fast and often dubiously, matching gaining lucre at speed.

clue.text: Drug that makes one live longer, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly signals that the phrase is to be heard spoken rather than read

parts.note: something extending life lets a person expire at a later date

explanation.surface: A medicine that promises to extend one's lifespan, according to rumour.
explanation.walkthrough: Making one live longer means one will 'die later', which spoken sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dilator can be a medication that widens blood vessels or pupils, so it is a type of drug.

clue.text: A soak's ending? What, in summer month? Do this then!

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces within the month

parts.note: May is the month in which summer begins in the clue's loose sense

indicators.note: ending picks out only the final letter of the word soak's

parts.note: eh? is an exclamation meaning what?

explanation.surface: A rambling exclamation about a drunk finishing up during a sunny month.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the proverb 'make hay while the sun shines': in a summer month, this is exactly what to do.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb urges seizing an opportunity, and summer sunshine is exactly the time for haymaking.

clue.text: Place reached by sea passage, we hear

indicators.note: we hear tells the solver to go by how the passage word sounds

parts.note: an aisle is a passage between rows of seats

explanation.surface: Someone describes a destination reached by a sea route, as rumoured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sea passage' looks like one phrase, but 'sea' belongs to the definition and 'passage' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An island is land surrounded by water, so it is reached across the sea.

clue.text: Old chap eating lunch maybe, one to perk up

indicators.note: eating has the chap enclose the food and numeral, holding them inside

parts.note: cove is an old-fashioned word for a man or chap
lunch is an example of a meal
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An elderly man having his lunch is somebody to cheer up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one' looks like part of 'one to perk up', but it supplies the numeral; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To come alive is to become lively or animated, which is what perking up means.

clue.text: Go wrong dealing with pub drink — being taken short within walking distance?

indicators.note: within puts the shortened drink inside the distance

parts.note: a mile is a distance one might walk

indicators.note: taken short means cut off at the end, so the drink loses its final letter

parts.note: shandy, beer mixed with lemonade, is a pub drink

explanation.surface: A drinker caught needing the toilet while walking spills his pint.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'taken short' is British slang for urgently needing a toilet, the misleading surface; here it means losing a last letter. Shandy is beer mixed with lemonade.
explanation.definitionFit: To mishandle something is to deal with it badly, so it means getting it wrong when handling.

clue.text: Little house with people not half dull

parts.note: HO is the short form of house

indicators.note: not half removes half of the word's letters, leaving the front portion

parts.note: humans are people

explanation.surface: A small home with its residents is described as boring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not half' cuts HUMANS to its first three letters, HUM; 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Ho-hum is an informal adjective for something boring or unremarkable.

clue.text: See 1
Fish gone off course, one no good for catching

indicators.note: for catching tells us the wanderer word holds the other pieces

parts.note: to stray is to wander away from the proper course
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An angler who has drifted off course is no good at catching fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A stingray is a flat-bodied ray with a venomous barbed tail, a kind of fish.

clue.text: See 6
No rebel, hard-working student said to be on the ball

indicators.note: said indicates that the three words are to be heard spoken aloud

parts.note: No, then Wat (Tyler, the peasant rebel), then swot (a hard-working student)

explanation.surface: A conformist, diligent pupil is said to be sharp.
explanation.walkthrough: Wat Tyler led the 1381 Peasants' Revolt; a swot is British slang for a studious pupil. Spoken, 'No Wat swot' gives the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To be on the ball is to be alert and well-informed, which this idiom also expresses.

clue.text: See 15
Like an old chapel in Wales Nye restored

indicators.note: restored suggests rebuilding the letters of the two names into a different structure

explanation.surface: Nye, a Welsh name, restored an old chapel in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'restored' rearranges WALES NYE. Methodist chapels, followers of John Wesley, are common in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Methodism was founded by John Wesley, so a Methodist chapel is described by this adjective.

clue.text: See 15
Underground passage undamaged with class heading off into it

indicators.note: into it places the shortened class inside the undamaged word

parts.note: whole means intact or undamaged

indicators.note: heading off removes the first letter of the class word

parts.note: form is a school class

explanation.surface: An intact tunnel with a school group setting off into it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' trims FORM to ORM, which goes 'into' WHOLE. FORM is the British word for a school class.
explanation.definitionFit: A wormhole is a burrow left by a worm, an underground tunnel or passage.

clue.text: Sixth sense employed to secure ring to be married

indicators.note: to secure has the two outer pieces hold the ring between them

parts.note: ESP, extrasensory perception, is called the sixth sense
used means employed
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A psychic used his intuition to get a ring and wed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be' is a link; 'secure' has the two outer pieces hold the ring between them.
explanation.definitionFit: To espouse is an old word for to wed, so espoused is a synonym of wed.

clue.text: Duke or count — he falls off gee-gee in middle of bog

indicators.note: falls off has the rider word drop away from the horse

parts.note: gee-gee is childish British slang for a horse
the letters of he come out

indicators.note: middle of takes the centre letter of bog

explanation.surface: A nobleman takes a tumble from his mount into a muddy bog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duke or count' looks like a choice of titles, but is the whole definition: the character is both in Twelfth Night. HE 'falls off' HORSE leaving ORS.
explanation.definitionFit: Orsino is Shakespeare's Duke of Illyria in Twelfth Night, also called Count in parts of the play.

clue.text: Lousiest material editor's chucked out

indicators.note: chucked out means thrown out, so the editor letters are removed

parts.note: worsted is a woollen fabric
ED is the usual abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: An editor throws out the shoddiest fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing ED from WORSTED leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lousiest is slang for poorest in quality, the same sense as this superlative of bad.

clue.text: "Jammy" ladies going to wicked city with a loss of love and common sense

parts.note: the WI, Women's Institute, is famous for jam making

indicators.note: with a loss of tells us to remove the love letter from the city

parts.note: Sodom was the biblical city of wickedness
love is zero in tennis, written O

explanation.surface: Lucky women head to a den of sin and lose their love and good sense.
explanation.walkthrough: The Women's Institute is a British women's organisation known for jam and Jerusalem; 'Jammy' (British for lucky) misleads. 'with a loss of' removes O from SODOM, leaving SDOM.
explanation.definitionFit: Wisdom is sound judgement, the same as common sense.

clue.text: Splits from son, always being held in scorn

indicators.note: being held in has the scorn word wrap round the other pieces

parts.note: diss is slang for disrespect or scorn
ever means always

explanation.surface: Someone cuts ties with a son who is constantly treated with contempt.
explanation.definitionFit: To dissever is to sever or divide apart, so it means splits.

clue.text: See 1
Characters enthralled by the beautiful goddess

indicators.note: Characters enthralled by says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Letters captivated by a lovely deity.
explanation.definitionFit: Hebe is the Greek deity of youth, cupbearer to the Olympians.

clue.text: See 6
African managed to seize rod of authority

indicators.note: to seize has the managing word grasp the rod inside it

parts.note: ran means managed
a wand is a rod carried as a symbol of office

explanation.surface: An African leader runs things by grabbing the sceptre.
explanation.definitionFit: A Rwandan is a person from Rwanda, a country in central Africa.

clue.text: Be boisterous, turning bad in swaying motion

indicators.note: in places the flipped word inside the swaying word

parts.note: rock is a swaying motion

indicators.note: turning flips the word for bad so it reads the other way

parts.note: ill means bad

explanation.surface: Someone becomes rowdy, turning nasty with a rocking movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' makes ILL into LLI, which goes 'in' ROCK.
explanation.definitionFit: To rollick is to behave in a lively, carefree and noisy way.
